paragraphs: Motor prostheses need to translate brain activity into movement commands while meeting the power constraints of an implanted device. Excess power dissipation can damage surrounding tissue. This paper investigates a computational step toward that goal: expressing a conventional movement decoder as a network of neurons that communicate through spikes.

The researchers first trained a Kalman filter to predict arm velocity. They then used the Neural Engineering Framework to map that decoder onto a spiking neural network. Their embedded MATLAB implementation contained 2,000 neurons and operated in real time, allowing it to participate directly in brain-machine interface experiments with a rhesus monkey.

In closed-loop use, the spiking decoder performed comparably to the standard Kalman filter. That result supports the feasibility of implementing this statistical decoding computation with spikes. The potential power benefit remains prospective: the demonstrated decoder motivates future neuromorphic hardware implementations that may provide the savings needed for fully implantable motor prostheses.
neurips-2011-a-brain-machine-interface-o.tldr: A real-time spiking implementation of a Kalman decoder achieved comparable closed-loop performance in a monkey brain-machine interface.

paragraphs: This paper studies active learning when examples arrive in a stream and their distribution can change over time. The learner must make predictions while deciding which examples deserve a label request. Distribution drift makes both decisions relevant: the examples encountered later need not follow the same distribution as those encountered earlier.

The authors analyze established disagreement-based algorithms, which use disagreement among candidate predictors to guide label requests. They prove upper bounds on two separate quantities: prediction mistakes and requested labels. This distinction matters because a learner's prediction performance and its demand for supervision are different aspects of success in the streaming setting.

The analysis covers both the realizable setting and a setting with Tsybakov noise, so its claims are tied to specified learning assumptions. The paper also proves minimax lower bounds, addressing the difficulty of the problem across learners. Together, these results provide theoretical guarantees for particular algorithms and fundamental constraints against which such guarantees can be assessed.
neurips-2011-active-learning-with-a-drif.tldr: The paper bounds prediction mistakes and label requests for active learning on changing data streams and establishes minimax lower bounds.

paragraphs: Estimating a changing stimulus from a sequence of discrete events is relevant to understanding how biological systems represent their surroundings. This paper examines that problem using point-process sensors with Gaussian tuning. Its focus is the estimation error of an optimal Bayesian decoder and how that error develops over time.

The authors derive an exact analysis of mean-squared error for this setting. Their treatment includes Markovian Gaussian processes and a class of non-Markovian Gaussian processes. The latter extends the analysis beyond the Markovian case without claiming coverage of every possible process. Tracking error analytically provides a way to examine the achievable limits of the specified state-estimation task.

A central finding is that some tuning width minimizes the error. Thus, the width of the sensors' response functions is a meaningful design variable, with the optimal encoding depending on the stimulus statistics. The result gives a mathematical basis for relating sensory encoding to properties of the environment being sensed.
neurips-2011-analytical-results-for-the-.tldr: An exact filtering-error analysis identifies stimulus-dependent optimal sensor tuning for specified classes of Gaussian processes.

paragraphs: Graph clustering can be expressed as cutting a graph into groups while balancing the resulting partition. Spectral clustering approaches this through a relaxed version of the graph-cut objective. The paper starts from a known weakness of that approach: the spectral relaxation can be loose, leaving a gap between the relaxed problem and the desired partitioning criterion.

Earlier work had established a tight relaxation for the Cheeger cut through a nonlinear eigenproblem. This paper broadens that result by characterizing all balanced graph cuts that admit a tight relaxation. The contribution therefore concerns which partitioning objectives can receive this stronger mathematical treatment, rather than only one particular cut criterion.

The resulting optimization problems are nonconvex and nonsmooth, but the authors provide an efficient first-order method that scales to large graphs. It also has a concrete initialization guarantee: from any supplied partition, it either returns a better partition or stops immediately. That guarantee concerns improvement over the starting partition, rather than a claim of globally optimal clustering.
neurips-2011-beyond-spectral-clustering-.tldr: The paper characterizes balanced graph cuts with tight relaxations and provides a scalable algorithm that improves its initial partition or stops.

paragraphs: Computing distances between high-dimensional vectors can be costly when many pairs must be considered. This paper develops a way to begin with inexpensive upper and lower bounds on Euclidean distance, then progressively improve them. The initial bounds use a proposed quantity called MS-distance, built from each vector's mean and standard deviation.

For n vectors with d coordinates, calculating those summary statistics takes O(dn) time. Once that preprocessing is complete, the initial bounds for a pair take constant time to obtain. The method also supports refinement: the bounds tighten monotonically and reach the exact Euclidean distance within d refinement steps.

The authors additionally analyze a random ordering of refinement steps. That analysis provides a justification for expecting tight bounds after only a few steps in a typical sequence, rather than promising that behavior for every pair. Experiments examine nearest- and farthest-neighbor search, illustrating applications where progressively narrowing a distance interval can help assess which objects are closest or most distant.
neurips-2011-convergent-bounds-on-the-eu.tldr: Mean and standard deviation yield cheap Euclidean-distance bounds that tighten monotonically to the exact distance.

paragraphs: Efficient coding asks how a sensory system can transmit information under constraints. Earlier tests using noiseless linear models of natural images produced oriented filters resembling responses in primary visual cortex. This paper investigates how the predicted representation changes when the model includes input and output noise, nonlinear responses, and a metabolic cost for firing.

The authors develop numerical methods that jointly learn each model neuron's linear filter and response nonlinearity. The objective balances information transmission against metabolic expense. On natural images, the learned filters have center-surround organization, while the response functions are rectifying. Separate On-center and Off-center populations each cover the visual space.

The Off-center neurons are more numerous and have smaller filters, matching a stated feature of primate retina. These results show that a richer efficient-coding model predicts retinal characteristics. Without noise, the method becomes a generalized form of independent components analysis and instead produces localized, oriented filters, demonstrating that noise changes the model's preferred representation.
neurips-2011-efficient-coding-of-natural.tldr: Adding noise, nonlinear responses, and firing costs to efficient coding produces natural-image representations resembling retinal receptive fields.

paragraphs: Stochastic gradient descent improves model parameters through successive updates. Running those updates on multiple processors introduces a coordination problem when they share the same parameters. Locking and synchronization protect shared memory, but they also impose overhead. This paper asks whether parallel optimization can work effectively without that protection.

The proposed scheme, Hogwild, lets processors update shared memory without acquiring locks. Processors may therefore overwrite one another's work. The authors support this design with theoretical analysis, algorithms, and an implementation. Their convergence result depends on sparsity: most gradient updates must change only a small portion of the decision variable. Under that condition, they establish a nearly optimal convergence rate.

Experiments show an order-of-magnitude advantage over alternative schemes that use locking. The finding combines a conditional mathematical result with a practical performance demonstration. Its significance is that preventing every conflicting update is not required for effective parallel SGD in the sparse setting analyzed, allowing the implementation to avoid expensive coordination.
neurips-2011-hogwild-a-lock-free-approac.tldr: Hogwild removes locks from parallel SGD and achieves nearly optimal convergence when updates are sparse, with large experimental speedups.

paragraphs: Independent components analysis can learn useful features without labels, but its standard orthonormality constraint makes overcomplete representations difficult to learn. These representations contain more features than input dimensions. Sensitivity to whitening creates another obstacle to using ICA with high-dimensional data. This paper changes the formulation to address both issues.

The proposed method introduces a robust, soft reconstruction cost. It allows highly overcomplete sparse features to be learned even when the data have not been whitened, and it works with existing fast unconstrained optimizers. The formulation also establishes formal connections between ICA and sparse autoencoders, giving mathematical support to a relationship previously observed empirically.

The reconstruction cost has an additional use in tiled convolutional neural networks, where it can prevent replicated features. The authors evaluate both highly overcomplete sparse features and tiled convolutional networks on object-recognition tasks. They report competitive performance across tasks and state-of-the-art test accuracy on STL-10 and Hollywood2, supporting the practical value of the modified learning objective.
neurips-2011-ica-with-reconstruction-cos.tldr: A soft reconstruction cost makes ICA suitable for highly overcomplete sparse feature learning, including on unwhitened data.

paragraphs: Sparse principal component analysis seeks directions of high variation that use only a small number of features. This can make the resulting components easier to interpret, but sparse PCA is commonly viewed as more computationally expensive than ordinary PCA. The paper shows that the sparse version can actually be easier in practice on large datasets.

The approach combines a rigorous feature-elimination preprocessing result with a favorable property of real data: feature variances typically decrease exponentially. That pattern allows many features to be removed before optimization. The authors also introduce a fast block coordinate ascent algorithm with substantially better computational complexity than existing first-order approaches.

Experiments use text collections with millions of documents and hundreds of thousands of features. They illustrate that sparse PCA can operate at this scale while organizing documents through components people can interpret. The result makes sparse PCA an attractive alternative to topic models for this purpose, while grounding the computational advantage in useful data structure rather than claiming that sparsity always makes optimization easier.
neurips-2011-large-scale-sparse-principa.tldr: Feature elimination and fast block coordinate ascent make sparse PCA practical for massive text collections and sometimes easier than ordinary PCA.

paragraphs: Local coordinate coding represents data using nearby anchor points, with the combination weights becoming the code. This supports modeling functions on nonlinear manifolds. The paper proposes a different geometric representation: encode data with orthogonal anchor planes. Its aim is to obtain useful local coordinates using only a few such planes.

The authors provide a linearization result for nonlinear functions satisfying the specified Lipschitz smoothness condition. The result controls the expected upper bound on approximation error for high-dimensional data. They also show how to learn the orthogonal coordinate system in practice by minimizing that bound using singular value decomposition, connecting the theoretical approximation criterion to a concrete construction.

For classification, the learned coordinates are used locally with linear support vector machines. In the reported MNIST experiment, 50 anchor planes achieve a 1.72% error rate, while local coordinate coding with 4,096 anchor points achieves 1.90%. This comparison demonstrates that the plane-based representation can provide a compact and effective alternative in the evaluated task.
neurips-2011-learning-anchor-planes-for-.tldr: Orthogonal anchor planes provide compact local coordinates with a smooth-function approximation guarantee and strong reported MNIST classification performance.

paragraphs: Many learning and signal-processing tasks become convex optimization problems with linear constraints. The alternating direction method can solve these efficiently, but its component subproblems are often easy only when the constraint mappings are identities. This paper modifies the method to handle the difficulty introduced by more general linear mappings.

The proposed algorithm linearizes the quadratic penalty term and adds a proximal term when solving each subproblem. It also adapts the penalty through a new update rule intended to accelerate convergence. The authors prove global convergence of this combined method, called LADMAP, establishing a theoretical foundation for the algorithmic changes.

The paper applies LADMAP to low-rank representation, a computationally demanding subspace-clustering technique. Combined with a skinny singular value decomposition representation, it reduces complexity from O(n³) to O(rn²), where n is the representation matrix size and r its rank. Numerical experiments report substantially faster performance than state-of-the-art LRR algorithms, supporting the method's use in larger-scale applications.
neurips-2011-linearized-alternating-dire.tldr: LADMAP combines linearized updates and adaptive penalties with proven convergence and faster low-rank representation computation.

paragraphs: Metric learning adjusts how distances between examples are measured. A common approach learns a linear transformation and then measures Euclidean distance in the transformed space. Kernelized methods allow a richer representation, but they introduce another choice: which kernel should define that representation for the learning problem?

This paper addresses that choice by combining metric learning with multiple kernel learning. Instead of selecting a single predefined kernel, the approach learns a linear combination of several. The same construction can combine information from different data sources. The authors present a general framework that can accommodate different metric-learning algorithms when those algorithms satisfy the required constraints.

Experimental evidence suggests that learned kernel combinations outperform both unweighted combinations and kernel selection through cross-validation. The contribution is therefore a way to make the representation choice part of learning the distance itself. The reported advantage is empirical, while the framework's applicability remains conditional on the constraints placed on the underlying metric-learning algorithm.
neurips-2011-metric-learning-with-multip.tldr: A general framework learns kernel combinations for metric learning, with empirical advantages over unweighted combinations and kernel selection.

paragraphs: Regression often represents data as matrices and applies transformations to vector subspaces. This paper develops a regression model for situations where both inputs and outputs are multidimensional. It uses tensor subspace transformations to describe latent variables shared across the two sides, keeping the multidimensional representation central to the model.

The method seeks latent variables with high correlation between the independent and dependent data. To estimate them, the authors apply multilinear singular value decomposition to a specially constructed cross-covariance tensor. The resulting framework also encompasses existing partial least squares and N-way partial least squares algorithms, connecting the proposed model to established regression approaches.

Simulations on benchmark synthetic data show advantages in prediction and robustness, particularly when samples are scarce. The authors also illustrate the method on predicting intracranial electrocorticogram recordings from simultaneously recorded scalp electroencephalogram signals. This application demonstrates the technique's potential for relating multidimensional measurements, while the synthetic experiments provide the stated evidence for predictive and robustness benefits.
neurips-2011-multilinear-subspace-regres.tldr: Tensor-based regression learns correlated latent representations of multidimensional inputs and outputs, with reported benefits especially at small sample sizes.

paragraphs: High-dimensional estimation can require relatively few samples when the underlying solution is structured, such as being sparse. This paper asks whether computation can benefit similarly. It focuses on greedy coordinate descent, which selects a coordinate to update, and identifies efficient selection as a way to weaken costly dependence on problem size when the solution is sparse.

The authors reduce greedy coordinate selection to nearest-neighbor search and develop several methods around that connection. They also introduce a form of greedy descent better suited to composite nonsmooth objectives, along with approximate variants. This connects a central optimization operation to tools for searching geometrically organized data.

A practical implementation combines greedy descent with locality-sensitive hashing. Even without tuning that search structure, it substantially accelerates ordinary greedy descent and outperforms cyclic descent when the problem becomes large. These findings support nearest-neighbor search as a useful computational ingredient, while also motivating further work on geometric search methods tailored to first-order optimization.
neurips-2011-nearest-neighbor-based-gree.tldr: Reducing greedy coordinate selection to nearest-neighbor search accelerates optimization, with particular relevance to large problems with sparse solutions.

paragraphs: Planning under uncertainty matters in applications such as robot control and wireless communication. Partially observable Markov decision processes describe the single-agent case, while decentralized versions handle multiple agents. For problems that continue indefinitely, policies can be represented by finite-state controllers. This paper introduces a periodic version of that representation.

The proposed controllers consist of layers connected only to the preceding and following layers. Construction begins with a deterministic policy for a finite planning horizon, which is converted into an initial periodic policy for an infinite horizon. This creates a route from a bounded planning problem to a controller intended for ongoing operation.

The authors then optimize the initial controller in two ways. A new infinite-horizon algorithm produces deterministic periodic policies, while a new expectation-maximization algorithm produces stochastic ones. The method reports better results than earlier planning approaches and can compute larger solutions than regular finite-state controllers, indicating that the periodic structure supports more capable planning within the studied framework.
neurips-2011-periodic-finite-state-contr.tldr: Periodic finite-state controllers support improved planning results and larger solutions for single-agent and decentralized partially observable problems.

paragraphs: An image collection may need to support searches for object categories that were unknown when its index was created. In this setting, examples defining a new category arrive only at query time. PiCoDes addresses the need for an image representation that is compact enough for large collections and useful for learning these later categories.

The method explicitly learns short binary descriptors at a chosen length, including codes as small as 16 bytes per image. Its optimization uses a bound tied to classification performance, making recognition quality part of code learning. Because direct optimization over binary features is difficult and nonconvex, the authors introduce an alternating scheme and a convex upper bound.

On Caltech256, 256-byte PiCoDes match the accuracy of the best-known classifier reported in the paper. They also reduce database storage by a factor of 100 and accelerate training and testing for novel classes by orders of magnitude. These results demonstrate a favorable recognition, storage, and computation tradeoff in that evaluation.
neurips-2011-picodes-learning-a-compact-.tldr: PiCoDes learns compact binary image codes that retain strong recognition accuracy while greatly reducing storage and novel-category computation.

paragraphs: This paper studies reinforcement-learning actors built from interacting modules. Rather than treating the actor as one indivisible decision-making component, it asks how each module can receive a useful learning update. The proposed coagent framework places these modular actors within an actor-critic approach, where a critic supplies a shared learning signal.

Each module's update requires only its own input, its own output, and the temporal-difference error broadcast by the critic. The rule therefore specifies a restricted information requirement for learning inside the actor. The authors present the rule, analyze it theoretically, and evaluate it empirically, making local module updates the central object of investigation.

The motivation is both computational and biological. Computing compatible features can become prohibitively difficult, creating a need for updates that use the available local information. Local updates with a broadcast critic signal are also desirable for making reinforcement-learning models more biologically plausible. The contribution is a class of algorithms designed around those information requirements for interacting modules.
neurips-2011-policy-gradient-coagent-net.tldr: Coagent networks train interacting actor modules using only each module's input, output, and a critic's broadcast temporal-difference error.

paragraphs: Probabilistic inference in a graphical model often computes information about every unobserved variable. A user, however, may ask about only a small subset. This paper argues that treating all variables uniformly can waste computation when the model is large but the query is narrow, and develops an MCMC approach that takes the query into account.

The method considers both the queried variables and their generalized mutual information with neighboring variables. This makes relationships to the query relevant to the inference procedure. The aim is higher computational efficiency by accounting for which parts of the model carry information connected to the user's requested quantities.

The authors report positive experimental results across a wide range of graphical models. These findings support query-specific MCMC as a practical approach to focused inference. The broader contribution is to make the requested output part of how computation is organized: the structure of a probabilistic model matters, but so does which variables the user actually wants to understand.
neurips-2011-query-aware-mcmc-fa51996d2a.tldr: Query-aware MCMC uses queried variables and their information relationships with neighbors to improve inference efficiency.

paragraphs: Crowdsourcing makes it possible to collect multiple labels for a dataset quickly and cheaply, but annotators differ in quality and expertise. Some assign labels randomly, potentially without examining the example. Such contributions can increase the cost of obtaining useful labels and degrade the consensus formed from several annotators' responses.

This paper focuses on ranking annotators by formalizing the notion of a spammer and defining an associated score. In the proposed scoring scheme, spammers receive values close to zero, while good annotators receive values close to one. The result is an ordered measure of annotator quality, rather than merely a final label for each data item.

That focus complements methods that estimate consensus labels while correcting for annotator bias. A consensus concerns what label an example should receive; the proposed ranking concerns the people supplying those labels. By making the distinction between useful and random labeling explicit, the paper provides a way to characterize contributors in a setting where annotation quality directly affects the value of collected data.
neurips-2011-ranking-annotators-for-crow.tldr: The paper formalizes random-labeling spammers and defines an annotator score that places them near zero and good annotators near one.

paragraphs: Learning features without labels can produce useful representations for classification, but many methods require extensive tuning. Sparse filtering is designed to make this process simpler. It has only one hyperparameter: how many features to learn. This concentrates the user's configuration choice on representation size while providing an efficient feature-learning procedure.

The method optimizes sparsity in L2-normalized features through a simple cost function. It does not explicitly build a model of the data distribution. The authors emphasize that the objective can be implemented in just a few lines of MATLAB, connecting the method's conceptual simplicity with a small practical implementation.

Sparse filtering also handles high-dimensional inputs and supports greedy layer-by-layer stacking to learn additional feature layers. Evaluations cover natural images, STL-10 object classification, and TIMIT phone classification. The reported results show that the approach works well across different modalities, supporting its usefulness as a simple feature-learning method beyond a single kind of input.
neurips-2011-sparse-filtering-6a72aca6e4.tldr: Sparse filtering learns useful representations by optimizing normalized feature sparsity, with only the number of features to tune.

paragraphs: The paper considers recovering a function's coefficients when only a small fraction of its available features have nonzero weights. Observations are noisy function evaluations at carefully chosen points. A central challenge is that the features may be arbitrarily nonorthogonal, so the recovery method must accommodate this lack of orthogonality.

The authors introduce Brownian sensing, an additional randomization procedure based on stochastic integrals. It produces a Gaussian sensing matrix with proven recovery properties independent of the number of sampling points. The sampling points themselves are uniformly distributed along a one-dimensional curve selected according to the features, linking the measurement design to the representation of the function.

For functions that are Hölder continuous with exponent at least one-half, the authors bound coefficient error by O(||eta||₂√N), where eta is observation noise and N is the number of samples. This error statement retains an explicit dependence on N despite the separate sensing-matrix result. Numerical experiments illustrate the proposed method.
neurips-2011-sparse-recovery-with-browni.tldr: Brownian sensing constructs Gaussian measurements for sparse recovery with nonorthogonal features and provides a conditional noise-dependent error bound.

paragraphs: A latent tree model connects observed variables through a structure that also contains hidden variables. This paper asks how to recover that structure from independent samples of the observed variables alone. Its setting includes multivariate linear tree models with continuous, discrete, or mixed hidden variables, encompassing several familiar graphical-model families.

The proposed Spectral Recursive Grouping algorithm builds the tree from the bottom up. Its central operation is a spectral quartet test: using second-order statistics, it determines the relative arrangement of four variables. Repeated local structural decisions form the basis of the larger reconstruction procedure.

The authors provide finite-sample bounds for exact recovery, showing how the required sample size depends on statistical and structural properties of the underlying distribution. These guarantees have no explicit dependence on the dimensionality of observed variables, making the method relevant to many high-dimensional settings. The qualification matters: the bounds still depend on properties of the distribution, even though dimension does not appear explicitly.
neurips-2011-spectral-methods-for-learni.tldr: Spectral Recursive Grouping recovers latent tree structure from observed samples using quartet tests, with finite-sample exact-recovery guarantees.

paragraphs: Some images are remembered more consistently than others across viewers, suggesting that memorability has properties connected to the image itself. This paper investigates which interpretable image attributes help characterize that variation. The goal is to move from observing differences in memorability to understanding the visual content associated with them.

The researchers extend an existing public memorability dataset with spatial, content, and aesthetic attributes, supplementing its object and scene annotations. They then use feature selection with explaining-away properties to identify a compact set of relevant attributes. This approach seeks an economical explanation of an individual image's memorability from its annotated properties.

The study finds that enclosed scenes containing people with visible faces are memorable, whereas vistas and peaceful scenes are less memorable. Unusual or aesthetically pleasing scenes do not tend to be highly memorable. These findings distinguish memorability from visual appeal or novelty and provide an early interpretable account of image-related memory differences at the intersection of cognition and computer vision.
neurips-2011-understanding-the-intrinsic.tldr: Interpretable image attributes connect memorability with scene content, while unusualness and aesthetic appeal do not reliably imply high memorability.

paragraphs: Annotating video requires deciding where an object is across a sequence of frames. This paper treats the choice of frames for human annotation as an active-learning problem. The aim is to obtain accurate object tracks with little user effort by selecting annotations that are especially useful to the current tracking estimate.

The selection criterion asks how much the estimated track would be expected to change if a candidate frame were annotated. Frames with large expected changes become valuable queries. The authors implement a constrained tracker and use efficient dynamic-programming algorithms to compute this expected change for possible annotations, making the query criterion operational.

The framework is demonstrated on four datasets, including two benchmarks built with key-frame annotations obtained through Amazon Mechanical Turk. The results indicate that equivalent labels could be obtained for a small fraction of the original cost. This supports choosing annotation locations strategically as a way to reduce effort while preserving useful tracking labels in the evaluated setting.
neurips-2011-video-annotation-and-tracki.tldr: Selecting video frames by their expected effect on an object track can substantially reduce the annotation effort needed for equivalent labels.

paragraphs: Recognizing a face from a new viewpoint requires handling appearance changes caused by three-dimensional rotation. This paper argues that the corresponding changes in two-dimensional images depend on object class. A transformation learned from rotating faces can transfer to another face, but the same transformation need not describe a different kind of object.

The authors test an architecture that uses previously learned, class-specific transformations to gain viewpoint invariance. In computational simulations, this approach works effectively within faces and fails dramatically when applied across object classes. The result ties the usefulness of transferred transformation knowledge to the class of objects from which it was learned.

On this basis, the authors argue that identifying a face across viewpoints from a single example view requires separate circuitry for discounting face rotations. Their resulting model agrees with physiological evidence for a hierarchy in face-processing regions, where viewpoint-specific cells feed downstream identity-specific cells with viewpoint invariance. The simulations support a computational explanation for specialization, while the circuitry claim remains the authors' interpretation.
neurips-2011-why-the-brain-separates-fac.tldr: Simulations support class-specific transformation learning as an explanation for specialized circuitry in viewpoint-invariant face recognition.
